title: What a Database Is
subtitle: Storage, lookup, concurrency, durability, and the guarantees above a file
objectives: Explain what a database gives you that a plain file cannot
Model data with tables, rows, primary keys, and foreign keys, and say why each fact lives in one place
Predict whether a query scans or jumps, and reason about what that costs
Explain durability and concurrency guarantees, and why the database is the hardest thing to scale

lessons.title: Why not just use a file?

exercises.title: A relational database coordinates durable records, concurrent changes, and queries
exercises.body: A relational database accepts writes and declarative queries. Depending on its schema and configuration, it checks constraints, coordinates concurrent transactions, records recovery data, maintains indexes, plans reads, and returns matching rows.
exercises.note: Writing application records directly to one file provides none of those policies automatically; concurrent or interrupted writes require explicit locking, framing, recovery, and indexing.

exercises.prompt: A query finds one email by scanning 1,000,000 user rows. Add a B-tree index on `email`.
exercises.afterStatus: INDEX SEARCH · roughly 20 comparisons plus the matching row lookup
exercises.result: The lookup stopped scanning the table
exercises.why: A B-tree index keeps email keys in searchable order, allowing logarithmic navigation instead of checking every row. Writes become more expensive because each insert or email update must also maintain the index.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: A query finds one email by scanning 1,000,000 user rows. Add a B-tree index on `email`. Place Email index, Users table. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Email query → Email index; Email index → Users table. That topology is the evidence for the answer: A B-tree index keeps email keys in searchable order, allowing logarithmic navigation instead of checking every row. Writes become more expensive because each insert or email update must also maintain the index.

exercises.prompt: Two signup processes both read the same `users.txt`, append a user in memory, then rewrite the whole file with no lock or atomic replacement. What can happen?
choices: Both are saved correctly — the OS handles it
The writes can interleave or overwrite each other, and one signup is silently lost
The file locks itself automatically
The second write is queued perfectly
exercises.why: Under the stated naïve read-modify-rewrite code, both processes derive output from the same old contents, so the later replacement can erase the earlier signup. File locks or an append protocol could prevent that specific race. A database packages concurrency control, recovery, and indexing as managed data services.

exercises.prompt: Which mechanisms does a database provide as managed data services that a basic file read/write API does not provide automatically? Select all.
choices: Safe concurrent access for many readers and writers
Finding one record without reading the whole file
Surviving a crash in the middle of a write
Storing bytes on a disk
exercises.why: A database packages concurrency control, maintained indexes, and crash-recovery logging behind its data operations. Applications can build locking, indexes, logs, checksums, and atomic replacement over filesystem primitives, but a basic file API does not automatically define or enforce those record-level policies.

exercises.prompt: Your process overwrites a record in place with multiple writes, using no write-ahead log, checksum, or atomic replacement. It is killed halfway through. What state can the file be in?
choices: Clean — the OS finishes the write for you
Possibly half-written and corrupt, with no record of what was in progress
It automatically rolls back to the previous version
Completely unchanged
exercises.why: Under the stated in-place protocol, the process can stop after only part of the record is written, leaving neither the old nor intended new value. Filesystems offer primitives from which safer protocols can be built; databases package logging, page checks, and recovery rules for this job.

exercises.prompt: `users.txt` has 10 million lines. You need the user with email `x@y.com`. What must you do?
choices: Jump directly to that line
Read lines one by one until you find it — up to 10 million reads
Ask the operating system to find it instantly
Nothing — files are searchable by default
exercises.why: Because the file has no access structure keyed by email, the program must compare the target with each line until it finds a match or reaches the end. The worst case reads all 10 million lines; an index can instead narrow the search to a small subset of records.

exercises.prompt: A ______ is a program built to store data safely and let many users query and change it at once.
choices: database
filesystem
cache
compiler
exercises.why: A database combines persistent storage with query processing and coordination of concurrent changes. Those mechanisms let multiple clients find and modify shared data while the database preserves its declared constraints and recovery guarantees.

exercises.prompt: So what's the honest one-sentence reason databases exist?
choices: Disks are hard to write to directly
Because storing data is easy, but querying it, sharing it between many concurrent users, and not losing it in a crash are all hard
They compress data better
They're required by web frameworks
exercises.why: The keyed answer names the three responsibilities that distinguish a database from raw storage: query execution finds selected records, concurrency control coordinates overlapping operations, and recovery mechanisms preserve or restore committed data after failures.

exercises.title: Relational tables connect facts with primary and foreign keys
exercises.body: A primary key uniquely identifies a row. A foreign key stores another row's primary-key value and can enforce that the referenced row exists. Normalization places a fact such as an author's name in one table while related books store the author's identifier.
exercises.note: Stable, meaningless identifiers reduce cascading updates when names or other attributes change. Their values still require lifecycle and generation rules.

exercises.prompt: Two users choose the same username at the same moment. Both application checks say it is available. Make the database decide the winner.
choices: Check availability twice in application code
Add `UNIQUE(username)`
Cache available usernames for five minutes
choiceFeedback: Both requests can still finish both checks before either writes.
The authoritative database serializes the competing inserts and rejects one.
Caching availability makes the check staler and leaves the write race intact.
exercises.afterStatus: USERNAME `maya` · one insert commits · one is rejected
exercises.result: The invariant is enforced at the serialization point
exercises.why: A pre-insert application lookup has a race between checking and writing. A database uniqueness constraint evaluates competing writes at the authoritative store and rejects the loser.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: Two users choose the same username at the same moment. Both application checks say it is available. Make the database decide the winner. Place UNIQUE(username). Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Request A → UNIQUE(username); Request B → UNIQUE(username). That topology is the evidence for the answer: A pre-insert application lookup has a race between checking and writing. A database uniqueness constraint evaluates competing writes at the authoritative store and rejects the loser.

exercises.prompt: You're storing users and their orders. Why put them in two separate tables instead of one big table?
choices: Two tables are always faster
So each fact lives in exactly one place — a user's email is stored once, not repeated on every order
There's no real reason; it's convention
To use less disk space overall
exercises.why: Separating users from orders stores the user's email once and links each order through a key. This normalization avoids an update anomaly: if the email were copied into 500 order rows, a partial update could leave conflicting values. The tradeoff is that retrieving combined user-and-order data may require a join.

exercises.prompt: Match each piece of the relational model to what it is.

pairs.right: A collection of rows of the same shape
The agreed shape of the data

exercises.why: A table groups records with a common structure; each row is one record and each column is one named attribute. The schema defines that structure, including types and constraints, so the database can validate writes and interpret stored values consistently.

exercises.prompt: What is a primary key?
choices: The first column in the table
A value that uniquely identifies one row — no two rows can share it
The password protecting the table
The largest column
exercises.why: A primary-key constraint requires a non-null value that is unique within the table, so one key identifies exactly one row. Other tables can reference that stable identity. Mutable natural values such as email addresses create extra update work when used as keys, so generated identifiers are often safer.

exercises.prompt: The orders table has a `user_id` column pointing at `users.id` — a foreign key. What does that buy you?
choices: Nothing beyond documentation
It links the order to its user AND lets the database refuse to create an order for a user who doesn't exist
Faster queries only
Automatic encryption of the column
exercises.why: A foreign-key constraint requires each non-null `orders.user_id` value to match an existing `users.id` value. The database checks that rule for every writer, preventing orphaned orders unless the constraint is disabled or deferred under explicitly configured conditions.

exercises.prompt: Why is having a schema useful? Select all.
choices: The database rejects malformed data before it's ever stored
Anyone reading the table knows exactly what to expect
It lets the database store and read the data efficiently
It makes changing the shape of your data effortless
exercises.why: A schema lets the database reject values that violate declared types or constraints, gives readers a shared description of each field, and enables type-aware storage and execution. Schema changes can still be expensive on large live tables when they rewrite data or require coordination with old application versions.

exercises.prompt: The ______ key uniquely identifies a row; a foreign key points at another table's row.
choices: primary
secondary
index
search
exercises.why: The primary key is the unique identity of a row. A foreign key stores another table's primary-key value and can enforce that the referenced row exists, allowing related facts to be linked without copying all of their attributes.

lessons.title: How the database finds your data

exercises.title: A declarative SQL query is compiled into an execution plan
exercises.body: SQL states the rows and columns required. The query planner uses table statistics, available indexes, and estimated operation costs to choose an execution plan such as an index lookup or table scan. The executor runs that plan and returns the requested result set.
exercises.note: Stale statistics or changed data distribution can make the planner choose a slower plan even when the SQL text and application code are unchanged.

exercises.prompt: Show the minimum components and flows that implement this mechanism: A declarative SQL query is compiled into an execution plan
exercises.why: SQL states the rows and columns required. The query planner uses table statistics, available indexes, and estimated operation costs to choose an execution plan such as an index lookup or table scan. The executor runs that plan and returns the requested result set. Stale statistics or changed data distribution can make the planner choose a slower plan even when the SQL text and application code are unchanged.

exercises.prompt: You run `SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'x@y.com'` — on 10 million rows, with no index on `email`. What does the database do?
choices: Jumps straight to the matching row
Reads all 10 million rows, checking each one — a full table scan
Asks the operating system to find it
Refuses to run the query
exercises.why: With no index whose leading key supports the email predicate, the executor has no direct path to matching rows. It performs a full table scan and evaluates `email = 'x@y.com'` for each of the 10 million rows, so work grows with table size.

exercises.prompt: Now: `SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = 42`, where `id` is the primary key. Fast or slow?
choices: Slow — same as scanning every row
Fast in a typical relational engine — primary-key enforcement uses a unique access structure for indexed navigation
Slow, because it uses the disk
It depends on the table's size, always
exercises.why: Typical relational engines create or require a unique access structure, commonly a B-tree index, to enforce the primary key. The engine navigates that structure and then accesses the relevant table or index page; this avoids checking every row but is not a zero-I/O jump.

exercises.prompt: Match each concept to what it means.

pairs.right: A question you ask of the data
Reading every row to find matches
Combining rows from two tables via a link
The database's decision about HOW to run your query

exercises.why: A query specifies the requested result, and the query planner selects an execution strategy. A full table scan tests every row; a join combines related rows from separate tables. Join cost depends on row counts, indexes, predicates, and the selected join algorithm.

exercises.prompt: Why is SQL called a 'declarative' language?
choices: Because it's verbose and hard to read
You declare WHAT data you want; the database decides HOW to fetch it
Because you declare variables before using them
It's just a historical name
exercises.why: SQL declares the desired rows and columns. The query planner selects the execution algorithm from available indexes, table statistics, and estimated costs, including scan order and join methods. Stale statistics or a changed data distribution can cause the planner to select a slower plan for unchanged SQL text.

exercises.prompt: A full scan must check 10 million rows. If the database can check roughly 1 million rows per second, about how many seconds does that one query take?
exercises.why: At 1 million rows per second, checking 10 million rows takes about 10 seconds. Concurrent scans compete for disk bandwidth, memory bandwidth, and CPU; once those resources saturate, requests queue and can delay indexed queries sharing the same database.

exercises.prompt: Which of these actually make a query faster? Select all.
choices: An index on the column you filter by
Fetching only the columns you actually need
Using `SELECT *` on a huge table
Filtering in the database instead of in your application code
exercises.why: A suitable index reduces rows examined, selecting only required columns reduces storage and network bytes, and database-side filtering avoids transferring discarded rows to the application. `SELECT *` can increase I/O on a wide table and may prevent an index-only scan.

lessons.title: Connection pools are capacity limits, not speed boosts

exercises.title: A pool bounds concurrent database work
exercises.body: Each connection can execute only a limited number of queries over time. Too few connections queue application work; too many can increase database CPU, memory, lock, and context-switching contention. The useful pool size is measured, not maximized.
exercises.note: Per-connection throughput changes as query cost and database saturation change.

exercises.prompt: The application sends 4,000 queries/sec. One database connection completes 20 queries/sec under this workload. Choose the *fewest* active connections that can keep up.
exercises.why: At 20 queries/sec per connection, 199 connections provide 3,980 queries/sec and queue work. Two hundred provide 4,000. More connections can increase database contention, so measured per-connection throughput is not constant forever.

exercises.title: A write-ahead log makes committed changes recoverable after a crash
exercises.body: Before acknowledging a durable commit, a database appends the change record to its write-ahead log (WAL) and flushes the required log bytes to stable storage. Modified data pages may be written later. During recovery, the database replays logged changes that were not yet reflected in those pages.
exercises.note: Sequential WAL appends are cheaper than forcing many scattered data pages. Group commit can flush log records for several transactions with one storage synchronization.

exercises.prompt: With synchronous durable commit enabled, the database returns success only after flushing the write-ahead log (WAL) to stable storage. Power fails immediately. Is the row recoverable?
choices: No — it was still in memory
Yes — recovery can replay the flushed committed WAL record
Only if it was small
Only if you waited a few seconds
exercises.why: Under a durable commit configuration, the database returns success only after the transaction's write-ahead log (WAL) record reaches stable storage. After restart, recovery replays committed WAL records whose data pages were not yet written, preserving the acknowledged row.

exercises.prompt: Build the durable commit path. The recovery record must be flushed before success; scattered data pages may be written later.
exercises.why: The database engine appends the change to the sequential write-ahead log and flushes the required log record before acknowledging a durable commit; dirty table and index pages can reach storage later. If success is returned before the log is durable, a crash can lose an acknowledged change because recovery has nothing to replay.

exercises.prompt: Two requests read a counter (value 10), each adds 1 in application code, and each writes back 11. What just happened?
choices: The counter is 12 — correct
The counter is 11 — one increment vanished silently
The database throws an error
The counter stays at 10
exercises.why: Both requests compute from the same value, so each writes 11 and the later write replaces the earlier result. This lost-update anomaly can be avoided with an atomic statement such as `UPDATE counters SET n = n + 1`, or with concurrency control that detects or serializes the conflicting read-modify-write operations.

exercises.prompt: Which of these are guarantees the DATABASE should enforce, rather than your application code? Select all.
choices: Uniqueness — no two users with the same email
Referential integrity — no order without a real user
Crash-safe durability of committed data
Business rules like 'premium users get 20% off'
exercises.why: Uniqueness, referential integrity, and durability are data invariants that must hold regardless of which application, script, or administrator performs the write. Database constraints and commit protocols cover all such writers. A changeable pricing rule is application policy and may differ by product context.

exercises.prompt: Your signup code checks 'does this email already exist?' and then `INSERT`s if not. Two signups for the same email race each other. What breaks?
choices: Nothing — the check handles it
Both checks pass before either insert runs, so you get two users with the same email
The database deadlocks
The second request is automatically rejected
exercises.why: Both requests can complete the existence check before either inserts, so each observes no matching row. A database `UNIQUE` constraint makes the decision atomic at insertion: one row is accepted and the conflicting insert fails for the application to handle.

exercises.prompt: You're recording analytics events at enormous volume — billions per day. Slide toward how strictly each write must be durable.
exercises.rightLabel: Batched / fire-and-forget (fast, may lose a few)
exercises.why: If the analytics use case explicitly tolerates losing a small number of events, batching acknowledgements amortizes storage flushes and raises throughput. The accepted failure mode is that a process or machine crash can erase the unflushed batch; financial or audit records generally require a stricter durability point.

exercises.prompt: Why is the database usually the hardest part of a system to scale?
choices: It's written in a low-level language
It's the stateful source of truth — app servers are disposable clones, but copies of data must agree with each other
Because it uses a disk
Because the software is old
exercises.why: The database is the stateful source of truth, so scaling it requires preserving data identity, ordering, and consistency across storage resources. Stateless application servers can be cloned because any instance can handle a request; database replicas or partitions require coordination and introduce lag, conflicts, or cross-partition work.

exercises.prompt: Two clinic processes append and edit the same patient JSON file concurrently. Updates disappear after interleaved writes. What database capability directly addresses this?
choices: Image compression
Transactional concurrency control
A larger filename
HTTP caching
exercises.why: A database coordinates concurrent reads and writes through transactions and concurrency control. A shared file offers no automatic lost-update protection or atomic multi-record change.
